topics.title: Quadratic Equations
topics.description: Solving quadratic equations by factorisation and the quadratic formula, and the nature of roots.

lessons.title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorisation
objectives: Recognise a quadratic equation in standard form
Form quadratic equations from word problems
Solve quadratic equations by splitting the middle term
Check roots by substitution
lessons.intro: A rectangular prayer hall has an area of 300 m², and its length is 5 m more than its breadth. What are its dimensions? If the breadth is x m, then x(x + 5) = 300, or x² + 5x − 300 = 0. This is a quadratic equation, an equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0. Quadratic equations appear in problems about area, motion, profit and many other situations, and they can have up to two solutions.
sections: Standard form

A quadratic equation in the variable x has the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b and c are real numbers and a ≠ 0. To check whether an equation is quadratic, simplify it and bring all terms to one side: (x + 2)² = 2x² − 3 becomes x² + 4x + 4 − 2x² + 3 = 0, or −x² + 4x + 7 = 0, which is quadratic. But (x + 1)² = x² + 5 simplifies to 2x − 4 = 0, which is linear, not quadratic. A value α is a root (solution) of the equation if aα² + bα + c = 0.
Factorisation method

If the quadratic expression can be factorised into two linear factors, we use the zero-product rule: if a product is zero, at least one factor is zero. To solve 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0, split the middle term using two numbers whose product is ac = 6 and whose sum is b = −5: these are −2 and −3. So 2x² − 2x − 3x + 3 = 0 → 2x(x − 1) − 3(x − 1) = 0 → (2x − 3)(x − 1) = 0. Therefore x = 3/2 or x = 1. Always check the roots by substituting them into the original equation.
Word problems

To solve a word problem: let the unknown be x, translate the conditions into an equation, simplify to standard form, solve, and reject any root that does not make sense in context, such as a negative length or a fractional number of people. For the prayer hall: x² + 5x − 300 = 0 factorises as (x + 20)(x − 15) = 0, so x = −20 or x = 15. A breadth cannot be negative, so the breadth is 15 m and the length is 20 m. Check: 15 × 20 = 300 ✓.
definitions: An equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
A value of the variable that satisfies the equation.
If ab = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0.
Writing bx as the sum of two terms whose coefficients multiply to ac.
examples: x² − 7x = 0 gives x(x − 7) = 0, so x = 0 or 7.

steps: ac = 6 × (−2) = −12; find two numbers with product −12 and sum −1: −4 and 3.

lessons.title: The Quadratic Formula and Nature of Roots
objectives: Derive and apply the quadratic formula
Calculate the discriminant
Determine the nature of roots from the discriminant
Find unknown coefficients for given types of roots
lessons.intro: Not every quadratic expression factorises neatly. Try factorising x² + 4x − 1: no pair of integers works. For such equations we need a method that always works. By completing the square on the general equation ax² + bx + c = 0, mathematicians found a formula that gives the roots of any quadratic equation directly. The formula also tells us, before solving, whether the roots are real or not, and whether they are equal.
sections: Completing the square and the formula

Completing the square rewrites an expression as a perfect square plus a constant. For x² + 4x − 1 = 0: x² + 4x = 1, then add (4/2)² = 4 to both sides: x² + 4x + 4 = 5, so (x + 2)² = 5 and x = −2 ± √5. Applying the same steps to ax² + bx + c = 0 gives the quadratic formula: x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] ÷ 2a. To use it, write the equation in standard form, identify a, b and c with their signs, and substitute carefully.
The discriminant

The expression D = b² − 4ac under the square root is called the discriminant, because it discriminates between kinds of roots. If D > 0, there are two distinct real roots. If D = 0, there are two equal real roots, both equal to −b/2a; the quadratic is then a perfect square. If D < 0, there are no real roots, because the square root of a negative number is not a real number. For 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0, D = 16 − 24 = −8 < 0, so there are no real roots.
Using the discriminant

The discriminant can be used to find unknown coefficients. For example, for kx² + 6x + 1 = 0 to have equal roots, D = 36 − 4k = 0, so k = 9. It also answers practical questions: 'Is it possible to design a rectangular park of perimeter 80 m and area 400 m²?' If the length is x, then x(40 − x) = 400, giving x² − 40x + 400 = 0, with D = 1,600 − 1,600 = 0. So yes, exactly one way: a square of side 20 m. If the area asked for were 500 m², D would be negative and the design impossible.
definitions: D = b² − 4ac, which determines the nature of the roots.
Rewriting a quadratic as a perfect square plus a constant.
examples: x² − 6x + 9 = 0 has D = 0 and equal roots x = 3, 3.
x² + x + 1 = 0 has D = −3 and no real roots.

worked.problem: Find k if x² + kx + 16 = 0 has equal roots.

lessons.real_world: Engineers check the discriminant to see whether a design is possible before building, for example whether a projectile can reach a certain height. Computer programs that solve equations use the quadratic formula because it works every time.
takeaways: x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/2a solves every quadratic equation.
D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: equal roots; D < 0: no real roots.
Set D = 0 to find coefficients for equal roots.

topics.title: Arithmetic Progressions
topics.description: Sequences with a common difference: the nth term and the sum of n terms.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Progressions and the nth Term
objectives: Recognise an arithmetic progression
Find the common difference
Use aₙ = a + (n − 1)d to find any term
Find the number of terms and solve related problems
lessons.intro: Reena saves ₹100 in January and increases her monthly saving by ₹50 every month: ₹100, ₹150, ₹200, ₹250, … Each amount is obtained by adding a fixed number to the previous one. Such a list of numbers is called an arithmetic progression (AP). APs appear in savings plans, the seating in a stadium, taxi fares and the rungs of a ladder that shorten steadily.
sections: What is an AP?

An arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term after the first is obtained by adding a fixed number, called the common difference d, to the previous term. If the first term is a, the AP is a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, … The common difference is found by subtracting any term from the next: d = a₂ − a₁. It can be positive (2, 5, 8, …), negative (20, 16, 12, …) or zero (7, 7, 7, …). To test whether a list is an AP, check that every difference between consecutive terms is the same.
The nth term

The terms are a₁ = a, a₂ = a + d, a₃ = a + 2d, and so on. Notice that the nth term contains (n − 1) common differences: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. This formula lets us find any term without listing all the terms before it. For the AP 3, 7, 11, …, a = 3 and d = 4, so the 20th term is 3 + 19 × 4 = 79. If the AP is finite, the last term is often written as l = a + (n − 1)d.
Using the formula

The formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d connects four quantities; if three are known, the fourth can be found. To find which term of 5, 11, 17, … is 125: 5 + (n − 1)6 = 125 gives n − 1 = 20, so it is the 21st term. To check whether 200 is a term: 5 + (n − 1)6 = 200 gives n − 1 = 32.5, which is not a whole number, so 200 is not a term. Problems often give two terms; for example, if a₃ = 12 and a₇ = 28, then 4d = 16, so d = 4 and a = 4.
definitions: A sequence in which each term differs from the previous one by a constant.
The constant d added to each term to get the next.
An AP with a last term.
examples: The odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, … form an AP with d = 2.

worked.problem: How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 7?

d = any term − previous term.
aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
A number is a term only if n comes out as a positive whole number.

lessons.title: Sum of the First n Terms of an AP
objectives: Derive the formula for the sum of n terms
Use Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d] and Sₙ = n/2(a + l)
Find a term from sums of terms
Solve practical problems on sums
lessons.intro: A famous story tells that young Carl Friedrich Gauss, asked to add the numbers from 1 to 100, answered almost instantly: 5,050. He noticed that pairing the first and last numbers, 1 + 100, 2 + 99, 3 + 98 and so on, always gives 101, and there are 50 such pairs. The same idea gives a formula for the sum of any arithmetic progression.
sections: Deriving the formula

Let Sₙ = a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + … + [a + (n − 1)d]. Write the sum in reverse order: Sₙ = [a + (n − 1)d] + … + (a + d) + a. Adding the two lines term by term, each pair gives 2a + (n − 1)d, and there are n pairs, so 2Sₙ = n[2a + (n − 1)d]. Therefore Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]. Since the last term is l = a + (n − 1)d, this can also be written Sₙ = n/2 (a + l), which is useful when the last term is known.
Using the formulas

For 1 + 2 + … + 100, a = 1, l = 100, n = 100: S = 50 × 101 = 5,050. The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2. For the AP 5, 9, 13, … to 20 terms: S₂₀ = 10[10 + 19 × 4] = 10 × 86 = 860. Sums can also give terms: the nth term is the difference between consecutive sums, aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁. If Sₙ = 3n² + 2n, then a₁ = S₁ = 5 and a₂ = S₂ − S₁ = 16 − 5 = 11, so d = 6.
Practical problems

A person saves ₹200 in the first month, ₹250 in the second, ₹300 in the third and so on. In two years (24 months), the total saving is S₂₄ = 12[400 + 23 × 50] = 12 × 1,550 = ₹18,600. In a school, prizes in an AP worth a total of ₹700 can be distributed among 7 students with each prize ₹20 less than the previous: 7/2[2a + 6(−20)] = 700 gives 2a − 120 = 200, so a = ₹160, and the prizes are ₹160, 140, 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Always identify a, d and n carefully, and check the answer makes sense.
definitions: The final term of a finite AP, l = a + (n − 1)d.
The sum of the terms of a sequence.
examples: The sum of the first 10 odd numbers is 10/2(1 + 19) = 100.
The sum of the first 50 natural numbers is 50 × 51/2 = 1,275.

topics.title: Introduction to Trigonometry
topics.description: Trigonometric ratios of an acute angle and their use in heights and distances.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Ratios
objectives: Define sine, cosine and tangent in a right triangle
Find the other ratios given one ratio
Recall the values for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°
Use the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
lessons.intro: Trigonometry means 'measurement of triangles'. Ancient astronomers in India and Greece used it to calculate distances to the Moon and planets. In a right-angled triangle, the ratios between the sides depend only on the size of an acute angle, not on how big the triangle is. These ratios, called trigonometric ratios, let us find unknown sides and angles without measuring them directly.
sections: Defining the ratios

In a right triangle ABC with the right angle at B, take the acute angle A. The side opposite A is BC (the perpendicular), the side next to it is AB (the base), and AC is the hypotenuse. The ratios are: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse = BC/AC; cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse = AB/AC; tan A = opposite/adjacent = BC/AB. Their reciprocals are cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A and cot A = 1/tan A. Also tan A = sin A/cos A. Because similar triangles have equal side ratios, the value of sin A depends only on A.
Standard angles

Some values are used so often that they should be remembered. sin 0° = 0, sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = 1/√2, sin 60° = √3/2, sin 90° = 1. The cosine values are the same in reverse order: cos 0° = 1, cos 30° = √3/2, cos 45° = 1/√2, cos 60° = 1/2, cos 90° = 0. Tangent: tan 0° = 0, tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3, and tan 90° is not defined. These come from an equilateral triangle of side 2 cut in half and from a right isosceles triangle. As A increases from 0° to 90°, sin A increases from 0 to 1 and cos A decreases from 1 to 0.
Identities and complementary angles

Using Pythagoras' theorem (AB² + BC² = AC²) and dividing by AC² gives the fundamental identity sin²A + cos²A = 1. Dividing by AB² gives 1 + tan²A = sec²A, and dividing by BC² gives 1 + cot²A = cosec²A. These identities let us find all ratios from one: if sin A = 3/5, then cos A = √(1 − 9/25) = 4/5 and tan A = 3/4. For complementary angles, sin(90° − A) = cos A, cos(90° − A) = sin A and tan(90° − A) = cot A, so sin 35° = cos 55°.
definitions: An equation involving trigonometric ratios true for all angles, such as sin²A + cos²A = 1.
Two angles that add up to 90°.
examples: In a 3-4-5 triangle, for the angle opposite 3: sin = 3/5, cos = 4/5, tan = 3/4.

lessons.title: Heights and Distances
objectives: Define line of sight, angle of elevation and angle of depression
Draw clear diagrams for height and distance problems
Use trigonometric ratios to find heights and distances
Solve problems involving two angles
lessons.intro: How tall is the Qutb Minar? How far is a ship from a lighthouse? Climbing or stretching a measuring tape is often impossible, but measuring an angle with a simple instrument called a clinometer and one distance on the ground is easy. Trigonometry then turns these measurements into heights and distances. This is how surveyors, engineers and navigators have worked for centuries.
sections: Elevation and depression

The line of sight is the line from the observer's eye to the object. When the object is above the horizontal level of the eye, the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight is the angle of elevation; we raise our head to look at it. When the object is below, the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight is the angle of depression; we lower our head. Because the horizontal lines at the observer and at the object are parallel, the angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).
Method

Draw a neat diagram with a right triangle: the vertical height, the horizontal distance and the line of sight as hypotenuse. Mark the known angle and sides and the unknown. Choose the ratio connecting the known side and the unknown: tan θ = height/distance is used most often, because the line of sight is rarely measured. Substitute standard values and solve. If the observer's eye is above the ground, add the eye height to the calculated height. Use √3 ≈ 1.732 when a numerical answer is needed.
Problems with two angles

Some problems give two angles. For example, from a point on the ground the angle of elevation of a tower's top is 30°; after walking 20 m towards the tower it becomes 60°. Let the height be h and the remaining distance x. Then tan 60° = h/x gives h = x√3, and tan 30° = h/(x + 20) gives x + 20 = h√3 = 3x, so x = 10 m and h = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m. Setting up two equations from two right triangles and solving them together is the standard approach.
definitions: The line from the observer's eye to the object viewed.
The angle above the horizontal at which an object is seen.
The angle below the horizontal at which an object is seen.
An instrument for measuring angles of elevation and depression.
examples: A kite string 60 m long makes 60° with the ground: the kite's height is 60 sin 60° = 30√3 m.
From the top of a 50 m cliff, a boat is seen at a 45° depression: it is 50 m from the cliff's foot.
